title: Be strong
hookLine: finishing a book, the congregation says: be strong, be strong, and we will be strengthened
tomorrow: Saba's bringing a cake. who throws a party for someone else's finish?

cards: The last stretch of a race, and strangers on the sidewalk yelling for runners they've never met. In the synagogue it happens at the last verse of each book of the Torah.
The reader finishes, and the congregation stands and calls out: chazak, chazak, v'nitchazek. Be strong, be strong, and we will be strengthened.

Noa has her own last stretch tonight: the final cast party before everyone scatters. Maddie and Jess still aren't speaking. Some hear in the words what Moses told Joshua at the end: "Be strong and of good courage."

teach.b: The sages give two answers, and both deserve a hearing. The first is Ben Zoma's, in Pirkei Avot: who is mighty? The one who masters his own impulse.

teach.h: RULING YOUR SPIRIT OVER A CITY.
teach.b: He leans on Proverbs, in the JPS translation: "he that ruleth his spirit than he that taketh a city." The best case for this view: every other kind of strength depends on it.

You can't help anyone if your own temper is running you. Strength starts inside, quietly, where nobody claps. The second answer comes from Avot de-Rabbi Natan, a companion to Avot: who is the mightiest of the mighty?
The one who turns an enemy into a friend. The best case here: self-control that never reaches another person is a strength kept in a drawer. Real might changes the room.
Two answers, inside and outside, and the tradition keeps both. Now listen to the words the congregation calls out again.

teach.h: BE STRONG; WE WILL BE STRENGTHENED.
teach.b: Be strong, be strong, said to each person standing there. And then: we will be strengthened.
Not I. We. Finish a book alone and you're done; finish it in that room and everyone gets stronger together.
Some readers hear both sages in that one line: master yourself, and bring others with you.

how: In Ashkenazi synagogues, when the reading of a book of the Torah is completed, the congregation stands and says 'chazak, chazak, v'nitchazek'; Sephardi communities have their own words of blessing for the reader.

o: be strong: said at the end of each book of the Torah
be quiet: said before the Torah reading begins
be blessed: said to a bride and groom at a wedding

games.q: two kinds of strong — tap the pairs.
p: mightiest: turns an enemy into a friend

s: the congregation's words end with 'and I will be strengthened'
v'nitchazek: and we will be strengthened.
the sages give more than one answer to 'who is mighty?'
Ben Zoma: one who masters himself; Avot de-Rabbi Natan: one who makes an enemy a friend.
chazak is said only once a year, at the very end of the Torah
it's said at the end of each book of the Torah.

games.q: your study partner says Ben Zoma's strength is too private to matter. make Ben Zoma's best case.
o: every outward strength depends on first ruling your own spirit.
private strength matters more because nobody sees it.
Proverbs says taking a city is the real test of might.
games.why: Ben Zoma quotes Proverbs: ruling your spirit is better than taking a city. without that, no other strength holds. the tradition keeps the other answer too.

practice: Stand up if you can, feet flat, the way a congregation stands at the end of a book. Let your weight settle through your heels. Say it once, out loud, at whatever volume the room allows: chazak, chazak, v'nitchazek.
Then stand still, and let the we in it include someone in particular.

wordCard.voice: Chazak: be strong. Called out at the end of each book of the Torah, twice for each person, then once more for everyone together.
